passage: Among the ideas that have shaped thinking about growth and fairness, few have travelled as far as the proposal, first advanced in the middle of the twentieth century, that inequality traces an inverted U as an economy develops. In the early stages, the argument ran, inequality rises as some workers move from a poor and fairly equal agricultural sector into a richer and more unequal industrial one; later, as most of the workforce has made the move and the new urban classes gain education and political voice, inequality falls again. The idea was offered tentatively, on the strength of a handful of national histories, but it hardened over the following decades into something closer to a law.

The mechanism at its core is sound as far as it goes. If a population is divided between two sectors with different average incomes, moving people from the lower to the higher will, by simple arithmetic, widen overall inequality for a time and then narrow it once the shift is largely complete. What does not follow is that this arithmetic governs the course of inequality in real economies, where it competes with many other forces. As data accumulated for more countries and longer periods, the curve proved elusive. Some economies grew rapidly while inequality stayed flat or fell; others saw inequality rise again after a long decline, a second upswing for which the original story had no room.

The damage done by treating the curve as a law was not mainly to economic theory. It was to policy. If rising inequality is a natural stage of development that growth will itself reverse, then governments in poor countries can be told to tolerate it, and governments in rich ones can be assured that any widening is a passing disturbance. Both lessons encourage waiting. Yet in the historical episodes that did show a decline, the fall rarely arrived on its own. It came alongside the spread of public schooling, the growth of organised labour, progressive taxation and, in several cases, the destruction of concentrated wealth by war and inflation.

A better reading treats the inverted U not as a path that development follows but as a record of what happened in some places when particular structural shifts met particular political choices. Read that way, the curve still teaches something, chiefly that the movement of people between sectors matters for how incomes are distributed. What it cannot do is assure a government that inequality will take care of itself.

passage: The ordinary picture of pain is that of a gauge. Tissue is damaged, nerves carry a report of the damage to the brain, and the strength of the pain reflects the size of the injury, much as the needle on a dial reflects the pressure in a pipe. The picture is intuitive and, for a great many everyday injuries, roughly accurate. A burnt finger hurts more than a scratched one, and both stop hurting as they heal.

The difficulty is that the gauge picture fails precisely where pain matters most. People sometimes suffer serious wounds in moments of danger or intense concentration and feel little until the moment has passed. Others feel vivid pain in limbs that have been amputated, where there is no tissue left to report anything. Most troubling of all, a large number of people continue to hurt for months or years after an injury has, by every available measure, healed. If pain were a reading of damage, none of this should happen. A pressure gauge that behaved in these ways would simply be sent back for repair.

An alternative account treats pain not as a reading but as a verdict. Signals from the tissues are one input among several; the brain combines them with context, expectation and memory, and produces pain when it concludes that the body is under threat and needs protecting. On this account, the soldier who feels nothing has a brain occupied with a greater threat, the amputee's brain is responding to a map of a body part that persists after the part is gone, and long-lasting pain may reflect a protective system that has grown oversensitive, raising the alarm long after the danger has passed.

This account is sometimes heard as a polite way of saying that the pain is imaginary, and patients with long-standing pain have good reason to be wary of anything that sounds like that. But the claim is the reverse. A verdict produced by the nervous system is as real as any other bodily event, and it hurts just as much. What changes is where treatment might be aimed. If the alarm itself has become oversensitive, then searching ever harder for a damaged structure, and operating on whatever turns up in a scan, may do little good, while approaches that address the protective system as a whole, through explanation, graded activity and attention to fear, may help where repairs to the tissues did not.

passage: Ask most people how to tell a language from a dialect and they will offer a test that sounds admirably objective: if two groups of speakers can understand each other, they speak dialects of one language; if they cannot, they speak different languages. The test has the appeal of turning a question that looks political into one that looks empirical. One need only sit speakers down together, the thought goes, and see whether conversation succeeds. The test promises, moreover, to spare the linguist from taking sides in quarrels that are seldom really about grammar.

Unfortunately the test does not deliver what it promises, and the reasons are instructive. Intelligibility is a matter of degree, not of yes or no; it varies with the topic, the speed of speech and the listener's experience; and it is frequently lopsided, so that speakers of one variety follow their neighbours more easily than their neighbours follow them. Worse, it is not transitive. Across many regions, a traveller passing from village to village finds that each community understands the next without difficulty, while communities at the two ends of the chain cannot understand each other at all. Where on such a chain does one language stop and the next begin? Intelligibility alone gives no answer, and the boundaries actually drawn on maps tend to coincide with something else entirely: the borders of states, the reach of a written standard, the language of schooling and broadcasting.

Everyday usage of the two words confirms this. The Scandinavian languages are counted as several, though their speakers can often converse, each using their own; the spoken varieties of Chinese are commonly called dialects, though many of them are no more mutually intelligible than languages that everyone agrees are distinct. In each case the label tracks not the distance between the varieties but the presence or absence of a shared written form, a shared state, a shared sense of belonging together. A dialect, in ordinary usage, is very often simply a variety that lacks the institutions which would have entitled it to be called a language.

It is tempting to conclude that the distinction is therefore empty, a piece of politics dressed up as science, and some writers have drawn exactly that conclusion. It does not follow. That a boundary is drawn by institutions rather than by sound systems does not make it unreal, any more than the border between two countries is unreal because no river marks it. Whether a variety has a standard spelling, a literature, a place in the classroom and a name its speakers use with pride makes a large difference to how it is learned, how it changes and whether it survives. A variety used in schools and courts acquires words for law and science; one confined to the kitchen and the field tends to borrow such words, or to give way to a variety that has them. Those are facts about the social life of a variety, not about its grammar, but they are facts.

The mistake, then, lies not in drawing the distinction but in where we locate it. The difference between a language and a dialect is not a property of the speech itself, waiting to be measured; it is a property of the arrangements a society has made around that speech. To see this is not to abandon the distinction. It is to understand that when a community campaigns to have its dialect recognised as a language, it is asking not for a correction of the linguistic facts but for a change in those arrangements, and that the request should be judged on those terms.

passage: Few words in the vocabulary of management carry as much reproach as slack. Idle machines, unfilled hours, inventory sitting in warehouses and staff whose days are not fully booked all appear, to the analyst armed with a spreadsheet, as resources that are paid for and not used. The programmes that set out to remove them, under whatever name is fashionable at the time, can usually point to impressive savings in their first year, and the savings are real. What such programmes measure less well is what the slack had been doing before it was removed, because its work was done in circumstances that the measurements were not designed to capture.

The first of those circumstances is the shock. A supply chain that holds no spare stock is cheaper to run on every ordinary day, and on the day a single supplier fails it halts entirely, because there is nothing between the failure and the factory floor. A hospital ward staffed exactly to its average occupancy works smoothly in most weeks and is overwhelmed in the week that an infection spreads. In each case the margin that looked like waste was a store of capacity held against an event whose timing could not be known, and its value appears only in the period that the efficiency audit treats as an exception. To judge slack by ordinary days is to judge an umbrella by the weather on days when it did not rain.

The second circumstance is less dramatic and perhaps more important. Organisations do not only respond to events; they also change themselves, and change requires time that is not already claimed. An engineer who has an afternoon free may try out an idea that no plan had scheduled; a manager with some unallocated budget can fund a small experiment without first writing a case for it that no one yet knows how to write. Most of these experiments come to nothing, which is exactly why a system that requires every hour and every rupee to be justified in advance will not permit them. The new products and methods that later look inevitable often began in precisely the margins that a thorough efficiency drive would have closed.

It would be naive to conclude that slack is always benign. Spare resources can shelter inefficiency as easily as invention, and a department with more staff than it needs may use the surplus not to experiment but to protect its own comfort or to fight for its standing within the firm. Some slack is indeed waste, and some of the people who defend it are defending their privileges. The critics of slack are therefore not simply wrong; they are answering a question that is badly posed. Asking how much slack an organisation has, and how quickly it can be reduced, treats a heterogeneous quantity as if it were uniform.

The more useful question is what the slack is for and who can see it. A reserve whose purpose is understood, whose size is reviewed and whose use is reported can be defended on the days when it seems idle, and trimmed when it has outlived its purpose. A reserve that exists only because no one has looked at it will be either preserved for the wrong reasons or eliminated by the first auditor who does. The aim is neither to maximise slack nor to abolish it, but to hold it deliberately, as an organisation holds any other asset whose returns arrive irregularly.

passage: Many historians regard the question 'what if?' as a parlour game, an amusement for the armchair strategist that has no place in serious scholarship. The past, they say, happened only one way, and the historian's task is to explain that way, not to speculate about others for which no evidence could ever exist. The objection has the appeal of modesty, but it rests on a misunderstanding of what historians already do. To say that a harvest failure caused a revolt is to say, at the very least, that without the failure the revolt would not have occurred when and as it did, or would have been less likely. Every causal claim carries such a counterfactual inside it, and the historian who refuses to examine counterfactuals has not avoided them; he has merely declined to inspect the ones he is already using.

The real question, then, is not whether to reason counterfactually but how to do it with discipline. Two constraints seem essential. The first is that the altered antecedent should be minimal and plausible in its own time: the most useful alternatives are those that people at the moment actually contemplated, such as a decision that was debated and narrowly taken, rather than those that require rewriting the character of a ruler or the technology of an age. The second is that the horizon of consequences should be short. Each step away from the altered moment multiplies the contingencies in play, and within a few years the alternative world becomes as indeterminate as the future, which is why the popular genre of imagining a whole century transformed by one changed battle is closer to fiction than to history.

A more searching objection holds that even a disciplined counterfactual smuggles in assumptions about how societies behave, about which pressures are strong and which choices are free, that cannot themselves be tested. This is true, but it is not peculiar to counterfactuals. The ordinary causal explanation rests on exactly the same assumptions; it simply leaves them unstated. What the explicit counterfactual offers is not freedom from such assumptions but exposure of them, so that a reader can see what the explanation depends on and dispute it.

Used this way, the counterfactual is less a tool for discovering what would have happened than a tool for testing what is claimed to have been bound to happen. Historians and politicians alike are fond of declaring outcomes inevitable. To show that a serious alternative was open, contemplated and within reach at the time is enough to defeat that claim, even when nothing reliable can be said about where the alternative would have led.

passage: Virtue ethics asks not what rule an action follows or what outcome it produces but what kind of person performs it. Its central concepts are traits of character such as honesty, courage and compassion, conceived as stable dispositions that lead a person to act well across a wide range of circumstances. The compassionate person does not help only when it is convenient or when someone is watching; her compassion shows itself in the market and at home, towards friends and towards strangers. It is this breadth that distinguishes a virtue from a habit, and it is what makes the attribution of a virtue a substantial claim about a person rather than a summary of what she happened to do last week.

In recent decades a group of critics, often called situationists, has argued that this picture is empirically naive. They point to a body of experimental work in social psychology, some of it now disputed, which has been taken to show that small and morally irrelevant features of a situation, such as whether a person is in a hurry or in a pleasant mood, predict whether she will help someone in need far better than anything we know about her character. If behaviour is driven so heavily by circumstance, the critics conclude, then broad traits of the kind virtue ethics requires are rare or nonexistent, and a theory built around them describes a psychology that human beings do not have. On this view, to call someone honest or kind is less a discovery about her than a story we tell to make her conduct look more orderly than it is.

The argument is more damaging to some versions of virtue ethics than to others. If the theory claimed that most people possess the virtues, the evidence would tell heavily against it. But the classical tradition never claimed this. It held that full virtue is difficult, uncommon and achieved, if at all, through long training, and that most people are a mixture of good impulses and weak resolve. Evidence that ordinary people are easily swayed by circumstance is exactly what such a tradition would predict. Indeed, much of the advice it offers, to avoid temptations rather than trust oneself to resist them and to choose one's companions with care, makes sense only on the assumption that character is fragile.

This reply, however, has a cost that its defenders do not always acknowledge. If genuine virtue is so rare that experimental samples almost never contain it, then virtue ethics can no longer claim the advantage it has often advertised over its rivals: that it describes moral life as it is actually lived, in terms of real people and their recognisable qualities. An ideal that almost no one embodies may still be worth pursuing, but it begins to look less like a description of character and more like a rule of the kind the theory set out to replace, a standard against which conduct is measured rather than a source from which it flows.

The situationist challenge, then, does not refute virtue ethics, but it changes what the theory can coherently promise. The theory can keep its account of the ideal, or its claim to realism about ordinary people, but it is hard to see how it can keep both. Which it should give up is a question that experiments alone cannot answer, since it depends on what we want an ethical theory to do: to guide those who aspire to goodness, or to describe those whose characters are already formed.

passage: In many parts of the world, groups of neighbours, co-workers or traders meet at regular intervals and each contributes a fixed sum to a common pot, which is then handed in its entirety to one member. At the next meeting the process is repeated and the pot goes to someone else, until every member has received it once and the cycle ends or begins again. The order may be fixed by lot, by agreement or, in some versions, by bidding, with the member who most urgently wants the money accepting a smaller pot and the difference shared among the rest. Such rotating associations go by dozens of local names, and for a long time development economists regarded them as makeshift substitutes for banks, ingenious but destined to disappear once formal credit reached the people who used them.

That prediction has fared poorly. The associations persist among people who have bank accounts, and they have travelled with migrants into cities where banks are on every corner. Their persistence is puzzling on a narrow financial view. For those who receive the pot early, the arrangement is an interest-free loan; for those who receive it late, it is a savings scheme that pays no interest at all, and that exposes them to the risk that an early recipient will stop contributing once he has been paid. A late member could, it seems, do better by saving the same sums in a bank, and an early member would be the obvious candidate for default.

The usual solutions to the puzzle point to discipline. Saving alone requires a resolve that many people find hard to sustain; a contribution owed to a group that meets every month, whose members will notice and remember a missed payment, supplies that resolve from outside. This is surely part of the answer. But it treats the problem as one between the saver and her own weaker self, whereas members themselves often describe it differently. What makes saving hard, they say, is not temptation so much as other people: the brother who needs money for a wedding, the cousin whose shop has failed, the neighbour whose child is ill. A sum in a bank account is visible to such claims and difficult to refuse. A sum owed to the association is not available, and saying so is an excuse that kin and neighbours recognise as legitimate.

On this reading the association is not a crude version of a bank but an instrument for managing obligations, one that uses a debt to the group to shelter money from other debts that are harder to decline. The reading also explains why the associations depend so heavily on the density of the ties among their members. The same social pressure that makes a refusal to a cousin acceptable is what keeps the early recipient paying; where members can move away without consequence, or barely know one another, the associations break down, and stories of a member who vanished with the pot are common enough to show that the risk is not imaginary.

None of this implies that formal finance has nothing to offer the people who join such groups, or that the associations are always wise; members of bidding versions sometimes accept heavy discounts out of desperation, and the losses from a collapse can be severe. The point is narrower and, I think, more instructive. The rotating association survives not because its members lack access to something better but because it does something that an ordinary bank account, by design, does not: it makes a sum of money socially unavailable. The question its persistence raises is less why the poor lack banks than what banks, as they are usually designed, lack.

passage: Public health suffers from a peculiar handicap: when it succeeds, nothing happens. A hospital can display the patients it has cured and a surgeon can point to the tumour she removed, but the officials who ran a vaccination campaign have nothing to show for their work except an absence. The measles outbreak that did not occur leaves no photographs, no grateful survivors and no line in the local newspaper. Success in prevention is a count of events that never took place, and such a count is always an estimate rather than an observation.

This invisibility is more than an inconvenience for those who would like credit. It changes how the public weighs risk. When a disease has been made rare, the vaccine against it becomes more noticeable than the disease itself. A parent who has never seen a child struggle to breathe with diphtheria, but who has heard about a neighbour's child running a fever after an injection, is weighing something vivid against something abstract. From where that parent stands, the calculation is not foolish; the danger really has receded from ordinary experience. What the parent may not see is that it receded because of the very programme now being doubted, and that it can return if enough people reach the same conclusion.

The same pattern appears wherever the benefit of a measure is an event that fails to happen. A food inspection service that keeps contaminated products off the shelves is easy to cut in a lean year, because the year after the cut looks much like the year before it. The costs of neglect arrive slowly, are spread thinly, and are usually blamed on something else by the time they become visible. Spending on treatment, by contrast, answers a need that is present and named. It is not surprising that budgets drift towards cure and away from prevention even when prevention is the cheaper way to buy the same health.

None of this means that the public should simply take officials at their word. Claims about disasters averted are claims about a world that did not happen, and they can be inflated by any agency that wants to protect its budget. The answer to invisibility is not deference but better ways of making the counterfactual visible: comparisons with places and periods that lacked the measure, honest accounting of the measure's own costs and side effects, and records kept carefully enough that a sceptic could check them. Prevention will never be as photogenic as rescue, but it can be made legible, and a public that can read its record is more likely to keep paying for it.

passage: The doctrine that a territory could be treated as belonging to no one, terra nullius, is often described as a lie that settlers told themselves. The lands of Australia or North America, the argument runs, were plainly inhabited; to declare them empty was either a culpable ignorance or a convenient fiction, and once the facts are acknowledged the doctrine collapses. There is something right in this, but it misdescribes the doctrine's real strength. Most of the people who invoked the idea of empty land were perfectly aware that others lived there. What they denied was not presence but a particular kind of relationship to the land, one that their own law was prepared to recognise as ownership.

The intellectual resources for that denial were readily available. An influential strand of early modern European thought held that property arose when a person mixed his labour with the earth, enclosing it, ploughing it and improving it; John Locke's well-known version of the argument drew explicitly on the example of America. On this view, land that was hunted over, gathered from, burned to renew its grasses or moved across with the seasons had not yet been appropriated, however long people had lived on it. The settlers' error, if it was one, was not a failure to see but a theory of what was worth seeing. Fences, fields and permanent buildings registered as use; songs that mapped water sources, rules governing who might hunt where, and the careful management of fire did not.

This matters because the doctrine has now been formally repudiated in several places, most famously when the High Court of Australia in 1992 rejected the proposition that the continent had belonged to no one at the time of British settlement, a proposition on which much of the country's land law had quietly rested. The repudiation was a real achievement, and it would be ungracious to belittle it. Yet the regimes of native title that followed typically require claimants to show that they have maintained a continuing connection with the land under traditional laws and customs, often to the satisfaction of courts that weigh written records and documented occupation heavily. Communities that were driven off their country, or whose practices were suppressed, find that the very dispossession they complain of becomes evidence against them: a broken connection, however it was broken, is a weaker claim.

In other words, the factual premise of terra nullius has been abandoned while something like its theoretical premise survives. Title still depends on displaying a relationship to land in forms that a court is equipped to recognise, and the forms most easily recognised are those that leave records. The burden has simply been reversed. Where the settler state once declared the land empty and left the inhabitants to prove otherwise in practice, the modern claimant must now prove, in a forum designed by the settler state, that the land was never emptied of them.

It does not follow that recognition is worthless, or that some purer form of restitution is readily available. Any legal system must have rules of proof, and claims that could be made without evidence would invite abuse. The point is narrower. A doctrine is not fully dismantled when its conclusion is reversed if the standard used to apply the reversal was shaped by the doctrine itself. To finish the work would require asking not only whether people were present, which no one now denies, but whose ways of being present count as having a place.

passage: For a long time the standard story about technology and pay was a story about skill. New machines, and computers above all, were thought to complement educated workers and to substitute for the rest, so that demand for the educated rose faster than their supply and the gap between their wages and everyone else's widened. Inequality, in this account, was the outcome of a contest in which schooling had to keep pace with machines, and the remedy was plain: produce more graduates. The story had the virtue of simplicity and the defect of predicting a smooth gradient, with the prospects of jobs improving in proportion to the schooling they required.

What many studies of rich economies in the closing decades of the twentieth century found instead was a hollowing out. Employment grew at the top of the wage distribution and, more surprisingly, at the bottom, while the middle shrank. The explanation that has largely displaced the skill story looks not at workers but at tasks. A computer, on this view, is good at carrying out any procedure that can be fully specified in advance, and the jobs made up mostly of such procedures, keeping ledgers, typing correspondence, inspecting items on a production line, happened to sit in the middle of the wage scale. Jobs at the top require judgement and the framing of problems; many jobs at the bottom, guarding a building, preparing food, helping an elderly person to bathe, require adaptability in physical settings that no program could specify. Neither kind of task was routine, and so both survived.

The task view is a real advance. It explains a pattern the skill view could not, and it shifts attention from the credentials of workers to the content of work. But its central category is less solid than it appears. Whether a task counts as routine is usually settled by asking whether it has in fact been automated, and a classification fixed by results cannot then be used to predict them without circularity. Tasks once thought to demand judgement, such as reading medical images or drafting standard contracts, are now discussed as candidates for automation, and if they are automated they will be relabelled routine after the event. The line between routine and non-routine describes the frontier of a particular technology; it is not a fact about the tasks themselves.

A second difficulty is subtler. Both the skill story and the task story treat technology as an external force that arrives and to which labour markets adjust. Yet which tasks are automated is a decision made by firms, and it depends on what machines cost relative to people, on how the tax system treats investment in equipment compared with spending on wages, and on whether managers regard workers as a cost to be reduced or a capacity to be developed. The same software can be deployed to remove a clerk or to let her handle cases that once needed a specialist. Polarisation, from this angle, is not simply what computers do to jobs; it is partly what a given set of incentives led firms to do with computers.

None of this makes the task view wrong, and it would be careless to replace one tidy determinism with another in which every outcome is a choice. Some tasks really are cheaper to mechanise than others, and no tax code will make a typing pool competitive again. The claim is narrower: that the shape of the wage distribution reflects technology filtered through institutions, and that a theory which treats the filter as fixed will mistake a policy question for a law of nature.

passage: Empathy enjoys a reputation that few other psychological capacities can match. To be told that one lacks it is an accusation; to call for more of it is to sound wise. Yet if empathy is understood in its strict sense, as the capacity to feel what another person feels, to be distressed by their distress and buoyed by their relief, there are reasons to doubt that it is a dependable guide to how we ought to act, however much it enriches how we live.

The trouble lies in its shape. Empathy works like a narrow beam: it illuminates whatever it is pointed at with great intensity and leaves everything else in darkness. It is most easily directed at people who are near us, who resemble us and who can be seen as individuals with faces and names. It is notoriously insensitive to number; the plight of one child described in detail can move us more than a report of thousands suffering in the same way, because thousands cannot be felt, only counted. A capacity with these properties will reliably favour the identifiable over the statistical, the familiar over the strange and the present over the future, and those are precisely the biases that moral reasoning is supposed to correct.

There is a darker possibility as well. Because empathy is felt for particular victims, it can be recruited against other people. An account of a single person wronged by a member of some group can stir a fierce sympathy that is then turned into demands for punishment of the whole group. The emotion in such cases is genuine; what is wrong is its range.

The obvious objection is that without empathy we would not care at all, and that a morality built only on principle would be bloodless. But this assumes that empathy is the only route to concern. Many people help strangers without imagining their way into the strangers' experience, out of a settled wish that others fare well, a sense of fairness, or the plain recognition that suffering is bad wherever it occurs. Psychologists sometimes distinguish empathy from compassion along these lines: the first means sharing another's feeling, the second means caring about another's good without necessarily sharing the feeling. Compassion, unlike empathic distress, does not exhaust the carer, and it can be extended to people one will never see.

None of this is an argument for coldness. In friendship, in parenting and in the consulting room, the ability to feel with another person is part of what makes the relationship what it is, and nobody would wish it away. The claim is narrower: that when we must decide how to allocate help across many people, or how to treat those we do not know, a feeling that shines only where it is pointed should be checked by judgement rather than trusted as the measure of what is right.

passage: Ask people to estimate a quantity they do not know, after first asking whether it is higher or lower than some number, and their estimates will drift toward that number. The effect survives when participants have watched the number being produced at random, when they are told it is meaningless, and when they are paid for accuracy. It appears among amateurs and professionals alike, in guesses about the age of a building, the price of a house or a reasonable figure with which to open a negotiation. That arbitrary numbers can move consequential judgements is now one of the least disputed findings in the study of decision-making. Why they do so is more disputed, and the answer matters more than it first appears.

The older explanation treats the anchor as a starting point. People begin at the number they are given and adjust away from it toward what seems plausible, but they stop too soon, at the first value that falls within a range they can accept. On this view anchoring is a failure of effort: the mind is a reluctant traveller who halts at the nearest acceptable station. The remedy follows naturally. Slow people down, ask them to think harder, give them reasons to care, and they will travel further from the anchor.

A second explanation locates the problem earlier. When we are asked whether a building is older than, say, two hundred years, we do not merely note the number; we test it, and testing a hypothesis tends to mean searching for evidence that would make it true. We recall the building's worn stone and its old-fashioned windows, and these recollections, now freshly available, shape the estimate that follows. The anchor does not set a starting point so much as select the evidence. If this account is right, effort is no cure, because a more diligent search conducted in the same direction only gathers more of the same evidence.

The two accounts are not exclusive. When people produce an anchor themselves, as when they start from a figure they already know and correct it for some difference, something like insufficient adjustment seems to occur, and in those cases encouraging effort does help. But for anchors supplied by others, which are the ones that negotiators, sellers and advocates supply deliberately, the evidence favours the selective account, and with it a different remedy: not to think harder about the number one has been handed but to think deliberately against it, by asking what would make it wrong.

passage: Ask people where they were when they heard of some great public shock, an assassination, a disaster broadcast live, the sudden death of a famous figure, and many will answer at once and in detail. They remember the room, who told them, what they were holding, the first thing they said. Such recollections have been called flashbulb memories, the name suggesting that a moment of intense feeling exposes the scene, as a flash exposes film, and fixes it for good. The people who hold them are rarely in doubt. Of all their memories, these seem the least likely to be wrong.

The difficulty is that when such memories have been checked, they have often turned out to be wrong in exactly the ways ordinary memories are. Researchers have questioned people within a day or two of a widely reported event and then again months or years later. The later accounts frequently differ from the earlier ones, sometimes in small particulars and sometimes wholesale: a person who first wrote that she heard the news from a colleague at work later describes, with complete assurance, watching it on television at home. Confronted with her own earlier account, she may concede that she wrote it while continuing to feel that her present memory is the true one.

What sets these memories apart, then, is not their accuracy but the confidence and vividness with which they are held; in these memories, conviction and correctness have come apart. One explanation is that the events are rehearsed endlessly. They are discussed with friends, revisited in anniversary broadcasts and retold until the story has a familiar shape. Each retelling is less a replay than a reconstruction, and the most recent reconstruction is the one that feels like the original. Emotion contributes too, but perhaps less to the record than to the sense of its importance: a moment that mattered seems as though it must have been remembered faithfully.

None of this means that strong feeling has no effect on memory. People rarely forget that the event happened, and there is reason to think that emotion sharpens memory for whatever is central to an experience while letting the periphery blur. The trouble is that the details we are proudest of recalling, the room, the messenger, the coffee cup, are precisely the peripheral ones. The practical lesson extends well beyond public events. Wherever memory is used as evidence, the vividness of a recollection and the certainty of the person reporting it are weaker guides to its truth than we are inclined to believe.

passage: It is often said that a book can be read for the first time only once, and the remark is usually meant as a lament. On a first reading we do not know what will happen; we are carried by suspense, surprised by turns we did not foresee, and moved in a way that, the argument goes, can never quite be recovered. Rereading, on this view, is a kind of nostalgia: a return to a place whose excitement has been used up, pleasant perhaps, but a lesser thing than the original encounter. Schools encourage the same view without meaning to, since a syllabus moves on once a book has been 'done', as though a single passage through it were the whole of the work. The lament has real feeling behind it, and anyone who remembers staying up late to finish a novel knows what it describes.

There is a case for the opposite view, that in an important sense only rereading is reading. A first reading is dominated by one question, what happens next, and that question consumes most of our attention. We skim descriptions to reach events, miss the significance of details whose importance has not yet been revealed and form judgements of characters that the book later overturns. Only when we know the ending can we attend to how the book reaches it: the early scene that quietly prepares a later one, the image that returns with altered meaning, the minor character whose remark, seemingly idle at first, turns out to state the novel's theme. Knowing the outcome does not empty these details; it fills them. Consider a novel built around a concealed secret. Read a second time, its hints, which at first seemed part of the scenery, stand out as hints, and the reader can admire the skill with which they were hidden in plain sight, a pleasure that the first reader, hurrying towards the revelation, could not have had.

Rereading also reveals a change in the reader. The novel read at fifteen and again at forty has not altered a word, yet it is a different book, because the person reading it has acquired experiences that let different passages speak. A story of a marriage that seemed, to the young reader, a tale of dull people becomes, to the older one, almost unbearably exact. Nothing on the page has moved; what has moved is the range of experience the reader can bring to it, and with it the passages that seem to matter. In this sense a book reread is a kind of instrument for measuring oneself, and the measurements are often humbling: we discover what we were once unable to see, and sometimes that the passages we admired most were the weakest.

None of this means that the first reading is worthless. It has a quality nothing later can supply, an innocence about what is coming that the writer counted on, and some effects are designed for it alone: the twist that recasts everything before it can surprise only once. Moreover, without a first reading there is nothing to reread, and the second encounter depends on the first even when it corrects it. Some books, indeed, are exhausted by one passage through them, and this is perhaps the most useful test of all. A book that offers nothing on a second reading was a mechanism for producing suspense, admirable in its way, while a book that gives more each time was something else. The difference between the two kinds is not visible from inside a first reading, which is one more reason to distrust the verdicts we reach there.

options.B: dwelling on descriptions in order to anticipate how the story will end.
options.C: noticing images that return later in the book with an altered meaning.

passage: Few management practices divide opinion as sharply as forced ranking, the system in which managers must place a fixed share of their staff in each band of a performance scale, so that some employees are always rated outstanding, most are rated adequate and a few are always rated poor, often with the expectation that the last group will leave. Its defenders make a reasonable case. Left to themselves, managers tend to rate almost everyone above average, partly out of kindness and partly to avoid difficult conversations, and a scale on which everyone scores highly conveys no information at all. A forced distribution, on this view, simply obliges managers to say what they already know.

The difficulty is that the system assumes far more than it appears to. It assumes, first, that performance within each team is spread along a curve, so that any group of a dozen people must contain its stars and its laggards. In a large population this may be roughly true, but a small team may have been assembled precisely because all its members are good, and forcing a distribution upon it manufactures distinctions that the work itself does not support. It assumes, second, that performance belongs to individuals, when in most organisations the results that matter are produced by people working together, and the contribution of any one of them is hard to separate from that of the rest.

The second assumption matters most, because of what the system teaches. If my rating depends on being ranked above my colleagues, then helping a colleague is a cost to me, and sharing an idea is a gift to a rival. The employees who learn this lesson fastest are not necessarily the most capable; they are the most attentive to how they appear. Over time, able people may also learn to avoid strong teams, since a good performer is safer among weaker colleagues than among excellent ones. A system introduced to reward merit ends by rewarding position.

It would be too strong to say that forced ranking never does any good. In an organisation where years of inflated ratings have left no way of distinguishing good work from bad, a single round of hard comparison may expose problems that polite evaluation had concealed. The harm comes when a jolt is turned into a permanent regime, and the habits of comparison it encourages become the ordinary way in which colleagues regard one another.

passage: A country that puts a serious price on carbon faces an awkward possibility. If its steelmakers, cement works and chemical firms must pay for their emissions while their competitors abroad do not, production may move to places where emitting is free. The country's own emissions fall, but the world's do not, and some of its industry has been lost for nothing. Economists call this leakage, and fear of it has been among the most effective arguments against acting alone. The obvious answer is a border adjustment: a charge on imports equal to the carbon price that would have been paid had the goods been made at home, perhaps paired with a rebate for exporters. Domestic and foreign producers would then compete on equal terms, and the incentive to relocate would disappear.

The proposal is simpler to state than to carry out. To charge an import for its carbon, one must know how much carbon went into making it, and that depends on the plant, the fuel it burned and the electricity grid it drew from, none of which an importing government can observe directly. Default values can be assigned by product and by country, but these penalise clean producers in dirty countries and reward dirty producers in clean ones. Letting producers prove their actual emissions instead requires inspectors or trusted certifiers inside the exporting country, which raises questions of sovereignty as well as of cost. Trading partners, moreover, are apt to see the charge as protection dressed in green, and some have a further complaint: that countries which grew rich by burning carbon for two centuries are now taxing the goods of countries trying to do the same, and calling it fairness.

There is also reason to think the problem itself has been overstated. For most industries the cost of carbon is a small share of total costs beside labour, transport, access to markets and the quality of local institutions, and firms do not move plants lightly. A steelworks embodies decades of investment in a site, a workforce and a web of local suppliers, and escaping a modest carbon price would seldom justify abandoning all of that. The evidence from carbon prices so far suggests less relocation than the warnings predicted, though the prices in question have mostly been modest and some heavy industries have been shielded from them by free allowances, so the past may be a poor guide to the effect of prices high enough to matter.

If leakage is less of a threat than feared, why does the border adjustment matter? Its most important effect may lie not in the trade it reshapes but in the decisions it prompts elsewhere. An exporting country whose firms face a charge at the border has a reason to prefer that its own government levy an equivalent price at home, so that the revenue stays at home instead of flowing to a foreign treasury. A border adjustment can thus act less as a wall than as a lever, drawing other countries towards carbon pricing of their own. Whether it does so, or instead provokes retaliation, depends heavily on how it is designed and presented. A charge that credits carbon prices already paid abroad, that measures actual emissions where producers can show them, and that directs some of its revenue to helping poorer exporters cut their emissions has a chance of being accepted as what it claims to be. One that does none of these things will be read, not unreasonably, as the protectionism its critics allege.

passage: Few settlement forms have been as consistently disparaged by writers as the suburb. For the better part of a century, novelists, critics and social scientists have described it in a nearly fixed vocabulary: monotonous rows of identical houses, lawns tended out of anxiety rather than pleasure, a life of commuting, shopping and television in which neighbours are near but never known. The suburb, in this account, is where individuality goes to be smoothed away. The striking thing about the indictment is not its severity but its uniformity, which ought to make us suspicious. A form of life chosen by many millions of households can hardly be as simple as the language used to dismiss it.

Part of the indictment is sound. A district built around the car leaves those who cannot drive, the young, the old and the poor, stranded in a landscape in which nothing is within reach on foot. Zoning that separates homes from shops and workplaces by law multiplies journeys and empties the streets of the casual traffic through which neighbours become familiar. These are real costs, and they fall unevenly. But they are the costs of particular design decisions, and the critique of the suburb has rarely been content to remain at that level.

Its deeper charge is cultural, and here it is weakest. It reads sameness of form as sameness of life, as if a street of similar houses must contain similar people living similar days; anyone who has knocked on the doors of such a street knows otherwise. It also tends to treat the wish for a garden, a quiet bedroom and a door one can close as a failure of imagination, when for families leaving cramped flats these were precisely the goods that city life had denied them. The critics, many of whom lived by choice in the centres of large cities, were often describing a preference they did not share as a pathology from which others suffered.

None of this requires us to admire the suburb, or to ignore the costs of a pattern of building that consumes land and fuel at a great rate. It requires only that criticism be aimed at what can be changed. The desire for privacy and space is not a defect to be corrected; the absence of a shop within walking distance is. A suburb with a small centre, mixed uses and streets that a child can safely cross would answer most of the sound objections without asking anyone to want a different life.

passage: Two drivers leave the same party, each having had one drink too many, and each drives home along the same dark road with the same degree of carelessness. The first arrives home without incident; the second, rounding a bend, strikes a child who has run into the road. Most people judge the second driver far more harshly than the first: he may face prison, while the first, if caught at all, will pay a fine, and the second driver himself will probably carry a burden of guilt that the first never feels. Yet the only difference between them is something neither of them controlled, namely whether a child happened to be on the road at that moment.

Philosophers call this resultant moral luck, and it presents a genuine puzzle. A widely held principle says that we should be blamed only for what lies within our control. If that principle is right, the two drivers deserve exactly the same blame, since their choices, their states of mind and their recklessness were identical. Our differing reactions must then be a mistake, an emotional response to a dreadful outcome that we wrongly dress up as a moral judgement. On this view, the honest course is to blame both drivers equally, and severely, for the risk each of them imposed on others.

This conclusion is tidy, but I think it is too quick, because it treats our responses to outcomes as noise to be filtered out when they may be tracking something real. The second driver has done something the first has not: he has killed a child. His relationship to the child's family, to the world and to his own past is altered in a way that the first driver's is not. To feel and to judge that he must answer for this is not simply to confuse bad luck with bad character. It reflects the fact that agency extends into the world, and that what we are responsible for includes, in part, what our actions actually bring about.

None of this licenses the opposite error of treating the lucky driver as blameless. He did something seriously wrong, and the fact that his drive ended well is no credit to him. The point is narrower: the control principle captures one important strand of our thinking about blame, the strand concerned with assessing character and choice, but it is not the whole of moral life. A theory that cannot make sense of why the second driver should apologise to the family, and why the first has no one to apologise to, has not purified our moral concepts; it has impoverished them.

passage: An old explanation of fashion holds that it trickles down. Those at the top of a society adopt a new style to mark themselves off; those just below copy it, hoping to borrow some of the prestige; and once the style has spread far enough to lose its power to distinguish, the people at the top abandon it for something else. Fashion, on this account, is a chase that can never end, because the very success of imitation destroys the value of what is imitated.

The obvious objection is that much of what is worn today did not begin at the top. Jeans were work clothes; the hooded sweatshirt was athletic gear; a great many styles that now appear on expensive runways were first worn by the young, the poor or the marginal, and were adopted by designers only later. If fashion so often bubbles up rather than trickling down, the old theory seems simply mistaken about the direction in which influence travels, and with it, one might suppose, about everything that followed from that direction.

But direction was never the heart of the theory. Its real claim was that fashion is driven by a double motive, the wish to belong and the wish to stand apart, and that the two cannot both be satisfied for long. That claim survives the reversal untouched. When a luxury house borrows the clothing of a street subculture, it is not abandoning distinction but finding a new source of it: the style carries a borrowed credibility that a conventional luxury garment lacks, and wearing it signals a knowingness that cannot be acquired simply by paying more. The members of the subculture, for their part, frequently drop the style once it appears in expensive shops, for precisely the reason the old theory would predict.

What has changed is the speed. When copies of a new look can reach inexpensive shops within weeks, visible novelty becomes a weak marker of status, since it is available to almost anyone almost at once. Increasingly, those who most wish to stand apart do so not by wearing what is new but by having had it first: by access to small releases that sell out in minutes, by acquaintance with designers before they are celebrated, by knowing what is coming rather than displaying what has arrived. The chase continues; it has simply moved to ground where the pursuers find it harder to follow.

options.C: it has spread so widely that it no longer sets them apart from others.

passage: It is tempting to picture the great periodic fair of the pre-modern world as a market that happened to be very large. Merchants arrived with bales of cloth, casks and livestock; buyers came from the surrounding districts; for a few weeks a meadow outside a town became a crowded street of stalls, and then it emptied again until the following year. On this view the fair existed because trade was too thin to support permanent shops, and it faded once towns grew large enough to sustain them. The account is not wrong, but it describes the visible part of the fair and mistakes it for the whole.

Much of what happened at a fair left no bales behind. Merchants who met there once or twice a year used the occasion to settle accounts that had been running since the previous meeting, cancelling what one owed another against what a third owed the first, so that relatively little coin had to change hands. Promises to pay at the next fair circulated as a kind of credit, and their value rested on the expectation that everyone would return. A fair, in this sense, was a calendar as much as a place: it fixed the dates on which obligations fell due and gave distant traders a reason to keep faith with one another. A merchant who failed to appear risked more than a season's sales; he risked his standing with every partner who had expected to meet him.

It was also a clearing house for news. Prices in distant regions, the solvency of a trading house, a harvest failure, rumours of war: all of this travelled with the people who came, and a merchant who stayed at home was not only missing customers but trading blind. The gossip of the fair was not idle. It was the means by which a scattered commercial world kept a rough common picture of itself. A thinly attended fair was therefore a loss twice over, since the absence of buyers was also an absence of reports, and those who controlled the best information often profited more than those who carried the most goods.

Seen this way, the decline of the great fairs looks different. Permanent shops certainly took over much of the retail business, but the deeper loss was of the fair's other functions, which passed to institutions that did not depend on bodily presence: banks that kept accounts all year round, regular postal services and, later, printed lists of prices. None of this means that fairs ceased to matter as markets; many survived for centuries as places to buy animals or household goods. What they lost was their role as the hinge on which a whole year of commerce turned, and that role had never been visible in the stalls.
